title: Punctuation: Every Mark and Why Writers Use It
summary: Every punctuation mark you need for Checkpoint 6, from full stops to semicolons, with the uses to learn, all the possible answers to 'Why does the writer use ___?', speech punctuation, apostrophes and practice.

blocks.text: 1. Why punctuation matters in Checkpoint 6

Punctuation marks are signals. They tell the reader where to stop, pause, add information, hear someone speak or feel a strong emotion. In Checkpoint 6 you meet punctuation in **both sections** of **Paper 1 (Non-fiction)** and **Paper 2 (Fiction)**:

items: **Reading (25 marks in each paper):** questions can ask **why the writer uses** a punctuation mark in a certain line, for example commas, an ellipsis, brackets or dashes, or ask you to find an example of a mark.

**Writing (25 marks in each paper):** **Grammar and punctuation** is worth **7 marks**. The examiner looks for accurate basic punctuation (capital letters, full stops, commas, speech marks) and a range of other marks used correctly.

blocks.text: The most common reading question looks like this: **Why does the writer use ___ in line X?** On this page, every mark has a box with **all the possible answers** you can write. Learn them.

blocks.title: The answer frame for every punctuation question
items: **1. Name the mark** and quote the words around it.
**2. Give its use** (from the boxes on this page): e.g. *to add extra information*.
**3. Give the effect** in this text: what the reader notices, feels or understands.
Example: *The writer uses brackets in line 4, '(the oldest tree in the town)', to add extra information about the tree, which shows the reader why it is so special.*

blocks.text: 2. Capital letters and full stops
A **capital letter** starts every sentence. It is also used for:

items: the word **I**: *Yesterday I went swimming.*
**names** of people, places, days, months, festivals, languages and nationalities: *Hassan, Cairo, Monday, March, Eid, Arabic, Egyptian*
**titles** of books, films and people: *The Secret Garden, Doctor Amin*
the **first word** inside speech marks: *She said, “**W**e are late.”*

blocks.text: A **full stop** ends a statement or a calm command. Forgetting full stops (and joining sentences with commas) is the most common mistake in Checkpoint writing.
3. Question marks and exclamation marks

rows: ends a question, including a rhetorical question
Where are my keys? Who wants to live in a dirty town?
shows strong feeling (surprise, excitement, fear, anger) or an urgent command

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a question mark (a question)? All the answers you can write
items: to speak directly to the reader and involve them
to make the reader think about the topic
to make the reader curious, so they read on to find the answer
a **rhetorical question**: to make the reader agree with the writer (the answer is obvious)
in a story: to show a character's confusion, worry or doubt

blocks.title: Why does the writer use an exclamation mark? All the answers you can write
items: to show strong emotion (surprise, shock, excitement, fear, anger)
to make the moment dramatic and grab the reader's attention
to show that something is said loudly or urgently (*Run!*)
to make the text lively and exciting, so the reader shares the feeling
in adverts: to make an offer sound exciting

blocks.title: One is enough
blocks.text: Use **one** exclamation mark, never *!!!*, and do not use one at the end of every sentence. Too many make your writing look childish and they lose their effect.
4. Commas
The comma is the most used mark after the full stop. It has many jobs. Learn each one with its example.

rows: 1. To separate items in a **list** (no comma before *and* in most British lists)
We packed water, sandwiches, fruit and a map.
It was a long, dark, frightening night.
3. After a **fronted adverbial** or opening phrase
In the morning, we left. / Slowly, the door opened.
4. After a **subordinate clause** at the start of a sentence (to separate the clauses)
When the bell rang, everyone stood up.
5. Before a **FANBOYS** conjunction joining two main clauses
I was tired, but I kept walking.
My uncle, a famous chef, cooked dinner.
7. To separate the **name of a person spoken to**
Mona, can you help me? / Thank you, Ali.
8. In **direct speech**, between the speech and the speaker
“I am ready,” said Omar. / Omar said, “I am ready.”
9. In **letters**: after the greeting and the closing
10. Before or after words like *however, yes, no, well*
However, the plan failed. / Yes, I agree.

blocks.text: **A comma can also show contrast**, depending on the context: *The house was small, but warm.* / *He was smiling, not laughing.* Here the comma separates two ideas that are different from each other.

blocks.title: Why does the writer use commas? All the answers you can write
items: **in a list:** to separate the items so the reader can see each one clearly
**in a long list:** to show how many things there are (how busy, crowded or full a place is, or how big a problem is)
**a pair of commas:** to add extra information about a person, place or thing without starting a new sentence
**after an opening clause or phrase:** to separate the clauses, so the sentence is clear and easy to read
**after an opening clause or phrase:** to create a short pause that builds suspense before the main action
**in speech:** to separate the spoken words from the speaker
**contrast:** to separate two different or opposite ideas
**many commas in a long sentence:** to slow the reader down and build up a detailed picture

blocks.title: The extra-information test
blocks.text: With a **pair of commas**, cover the words between them. If the sentence still makes complete sense, the commas are around extra information. *My uncle, a famous chef, cooked dinner.* → *My uncle cooked dinner.* ✓

blocks.title: The comma splice
blocks.text: Never join two complete sentences with only a comma. *It was late, we went home.* ✗ Write *It was late, so we went home.* or *It was late. We went home.* ✓
5. Apostrophes
The apostrophe ( ' ) has **two** jobs: **omission** (missing letters) and **possession** (belonging).
**Job 1: Omission (contractions).** The apostrophe goes exactly where the letters are missing.
**Job 2: Possession (belonging).**

rows: the girl's bag (one girl) / the dog's bone
One owner ending in s: add **'s**
More than one owner, plural ends in s: add **'** only
the girls' bags (many girls) / my parents' car
Plural that does not end in s: add **'s**
the children's toys / the men's shoes / the people's choice
Two people sharing one thing: 's on the last name only

blocks.title: Apostrophe traps
items: **Never** use an apostrophe for a simple plural: *apple's for sale* ✗ → *apples for sale* ✓
**its** = belonging to it (*The cat licked its paw.*) / **it's** = it is or it has (*It's raining.*)
**your** = belonging to you / **you're** = you are
**their** = belonging to them / **they're** = they are / **there** = a place
**whose** = belonging to whom / **who's** = who is

blocks.title: Why does the writer use apostrophes for contractions (don't, I'm, can't)? All the answers you can write
items: to make the writing sound **informal**, chatty and friendly, like someone talking
to make speech or a character's thoughts sound natural and realistic
to suit the audience, for example in an informal email, diary, blog or a magazine for children

blocks.title: Formal writing
blocks.text: In formal writing (a formal letter, a report, a balanced argument) use full forms: *do not, it is, we have*. In informal writing and in speech, contractions are fine.
6. Inverted commas (speech marks)
Inverted commas (“ ” or ‘ ’) have **four** uses that you must know:

rows: 1. **Direct speech**: the exact words someone says
2. A **quotation**: the exact words of someone, copied from somewhere else
The head teacher called the show “the best we have ever had”.
3. Words that are **not meant literally** (not the real meaning, and sometimes the writer does not believe them)
Our “holiday” was a week of rain and cold. (It did not feel like a real holiday.)
4. A name that is **not the real name** (a nickname or made-up name)
Everyone called the old car “The Rocket”.

blocks.title: Why does the writer use inverted commas? All the answers you can write
items: **speech:** to show the exact words a character says, so the reader hears them directly and the scene feels real
**quotation:** to show these are someone else's exact words, which makes the information more believable (e.g. an expert's opinion in a news report)
**not literal:** to show the word is not meant in its real meaning, often to be funny or to show the writer does not really believe it
**not the real name:** to show this is a nickname or a made-up name, not the real name

blocks.text: 7. How to punctuate direct speech
Speech punctuation is checked in **every** story you write in Paper 2, and quotations often appear in Paper 1 news reports. Follow these rules exactly.

items: Put the **exact spoken words** inside inverted commas.
Start the spoken words with a **capital letter**.
Put the punctuation that ends the speech (**, . ? !**) **inside** the closing inverted commas.
If the speaker comes **after** the speech, end the speech with a **comma** (not a full stop), or with ? or ! : *“We are lost,” said Hana.* / *“Are we lost?” asked Hana.*
If the speaker comes **before** the speech, put a **comma** after the speaker: *Hana said, “We are lost.”*
**Split speech** in one sentence: *“If we hurry,” said Hana, “we can still catch the bus.”* (the second part starts with a small letter, because it is the same sentence)
Start a **new line** every time a **new person** speaks.

blocks.text: **Model of a correctly punctuated conversation (original):**
“Where did you find this map?” asked Karim, turning it over in his hands.
“In Grandad's old trunk,” Nour replied. “It was hidden under a pile of letters.”
Karim pointed at a red cross near the river. “Then that,” he said slowly, “must be where the treasure is buried!”

rows: “Let's go,” said Mona, “It is late.” (two sentences)
Two speakers on the same line

blocks.title: Direct speech or reported speech?
blocks.text: **Direct speech** uses the exact words and inverted commas: *Ali said, “I am tired.”* **Reported speech** retells what was said, with **no inverted commas**: *Ali said that he was tired.* (See the Grammar in Use page for how to change one into the other.)
8. The colon ( : )
A colon usually comes after a **complete sentence**. It tells the reader: *here comes something that follows from what I have just said.* The colon has **four** uses:

rows: You will need three things: a torch, a rope and a map.
We stayed inside all day: it was far too hot to go out.
3. To give **emphasis** (to make what follows stand out)
There was only one person who could help: Grandma.
The museum has a new exhibition: the treasures of ancient Egypt.

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a colon? All the answers you can write
items: **list:** to introduce a list, so the reader can see all the items clearly
**explanation:** to introduce an explanation of the idea before it (it tells us why or how)
**emphasis:** to make the words after it stand out and seem important
**emphasis:** to create a small pause before the key words, which can build suspense
**extra information:** to add extra information about the idea before it

blocks.title: Other places you will see a colon
blocks.text: Colons are also used in times (*7:30*) and in playscripts, after a character's name (*NOUR: Who's there?*). These are layout uses, not effects.
9. The semicolon ( ; )
The semicolon has **one** use: it **joins two independent clauses** (two complete sentences) that are **closely related**. Each side must be a complete sentence on its own.

items: *The rain had stopped; the children ran outside to play.*
*Omar loves football; he plays every afternoon.*
*The cave was silent; nobody dared to speak.*

blocks.title: The semicolon test
blocks.text: Replace the semicolon with a full stop. If you now have **two correct sentences**, the semicolon is right. *Omar loves football. He plays every afternoon.* ✓ If one side is not a complete sentence, the semicolon is wrong: *Because it rained; we stayed in.* ✗

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a semicolon? All the answers you can write
items: to join two independent clauses that are closely related
to show the reader that the two ideas are connected and belong together
to keep the two ideas in one sentence, so the reader reads them together and sees the link
to avoid two short, choppy sentences and make the writing flow smoothly

blocks.title: Do not
items: Do not use a semicolon before a list (use a colon).
Do not use a semicolon after a subordinate clause (*When I arrived; ...* ✗).
Do not use a semicolon with *and, but, so* between the clauses: either the conjunction or the semicolon.

blocks.text: 10. Dashes ( – )
A dash ( – ) is longer than a hyphen and has a space on each side. Writers use dashes in **two ways**: a **pair** of dashes or a **single** dash.

rows: **extra information** in the middle of a sentence
My best friend – the boy who lives next door – is moving to Alexandria.
**emphasis**: makes the words after it stand out, often something dramatic or surprising
We opened the box and found nothing inside – not even a note.
**interruption** in the middle of speech, when someone is cut off or stops suddenly

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a pair of dashes? All the answers you can write
items: to add extra information about the person, place or thing in the sentence
the extra information stands out more than it would with commas, so the reader notices it

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a single dash? All the answers you can write
items: **emphasis:** to make the words after it stand out and seem important
**emphasis:** to create a pause before a surprising or dramatic ending, which shocks the reader or builds suspense
**interruption:** to show that a speaker is cut off or interrupted while speaking
**interruption:** to show a character stopping suddenly (because of fear, shock or another person), which makes the speech sound real and creates tension

blocks.text: 11. Brackets ( )
Brackets always come in pairs. They have **one** use: to add **extra information**. If you take the brackets and the words inside away, the sentence still makes sense.

items: *The Nile (the longest river in Africa) flows through eleven countries.*
*Our teacher (who is usually very calm) shouted with joy.*
*Tickets cost 50 pounds (children under five go free).*

blocks.title: Why does the writer use brackets? All the answers you can write
items: to add extra information without interrupting the main sentence
to explain a word or give a detail (a date, a number, an example) that helps the reader understand
to show the information is less important, like a quick side comment
in informal writing: the side comment can make the writer sound chatty and friendly, as if talking to the reader

blocks.title: Commas, dashes or brackets?
blocks.text: All three can mark **extra information** in the middle of a sentence. **Commas** are the gentlest, **brackets** make it a quiet side comment, and **dashes** make it stand out the most. Choosing different ones shows the examiner a range of punctuation.
12. Ellipsis ( ... )
An ellipsis is **three dots**: never two, never five. It has **three** uses:

rows: 1. **Incomplete information**: words or ideas are left out, or a sentence trails off and the reader must guess the rest
And they lived happily ever after... or did they?
2. **Suspense / a pause**: makes the reader wait
Slowly, the door creaked open... and there stood a tall, dark figure.
3. **Interruption**: speech breaks off or someone hesitates
“I was just... I mean, I didn't...” stammered Yousef.

blocks.title: Why does the writer use an ellipsis? All the answers you can write
items: **incomplete information:** to show that something is left out or unfinished, so the reader has to imagine the rest
**incomplete information:** to leave the reader wondering, which creates mystery
**suspense / pause:** to make the reader pause and wait, which builds suspense and tension before something important happens
**suspense / pause:** at the end of a paragraph or chapter (a cliffhanger), to make the reader want to read on
**interruption:** to show a character is interrupted, or hesitates, because they are nervous, scared, unsure or upset
**interruption:** to show speech trailing off, which makes it sound realistic

blocks.title: Do not overuse it
blocks.text: One ellipsis at the most suspenseful moment is powerful. An ellipsis at the end of every sentence loses its effect and looks careless.
13. The hyphen ( - )
A hyphen is **shorter** than a dash and has **no spaces** around it. It **joins** words or parts of words.

rows: 1. To join words that make **one describing word** before a noun
a well-known writer / a ten-year-old boy / a man-eating shark
2. In **numbers** from twenty-one to ninety-nine, and in fractions
3. With some **prefixes**, especially to avoid two vowels together or confusion
re-enter / co-operate / ex-teacher / re-cover (cover again) is different from recover (get better)

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a hyphen? All the answers you can write
items: to join words into one describing word, so the description is clear and compact
to make the meaning clear and avoid confusion (*a man-eating shark* is very different from *a man eating shark*)
in speech (*b-b-but*): to show the character is stammering because they are scared, nervous or cold

blocks.text: 14. Bullet points
Bullet points are a **layout feature** of non-fiction texts (Paper 1), such as leaflets, instructions, information texts and reports. Each bullet point is one short item or idea.

items: Keep each bullet short.
Start each bullet in the same way (all verbs, or all nouns).
Introduce the bullet list with a short sentence ending in a colon.

blocks.title: Why does the writer use bullet points? All the answers you can write
items: to break information into short, clear points that are easy to read
to help the reader find information quickly
to make important points stand out
to organise information and avoid long, heavy paragraphs
to suit the text type (a leaflet, instructions or a fact sheet)

blocks.text: 15. All the marks in one table

rows: ends a statement or a calm command
ends a question, including a rhetorical question
lists / adjectives / after an opening phrase or clause / before FANBOYS / pair of commas = extra information / name of the person spoken to / speech / can show contrast by context
direct speech / a quotation by someone / not the literal meaning / not the real name
joins two independent, closely related clauses (only this use)
joins words into one / numbers / prefixes / stammering
short, clear, easy-to-find points in non-fiction

blocks.title: أهم قواعد علامات الترقيم كما ندرّسها
items: الـ semicolon له استخدام واحد فقط: يربط جملتين كاملتين مرتبطتين ببعض. لا تكتب أنه يُظهر تضادًا، ولا تستخدمه في القوائم.
الـ colon: قائمة، أو شرح، أو تأكيد (emphasis)، أو معلومة إضافية.
زوج الـ dashes = معلومة إضافية دائمًا. الـ dash الواحدة = تأكيد، أو مقاطعة في الكلام.
الأقواس (brackets) = معلومة إضافية. الـ ellipsis = معلومة ناقصة، أو تشويق/توقف، أو مقاطعة.

blocks.text: 16. Worked exam-style example
Read this original extract. The line numbers are given as they would be in the exam.
**Line 1:** Every Friday, my grandfather – the strongest man I have ever known – took me fishing.
**Line 2:** We always took the same things: two rods, a bucket and a bag of bread.
**Line 3:** One morning, the line pulled hard; the rod bent like a bow.
**Line 4:** “Hold on, Sami!” Grandad shouted. “Don't let it –”
**Line 5:** The line snapped. The water went still... and then something huge rose to the surface.

items.q: Why does the writer use a pair of dashes in line 1? (1 mark)
items.a: To add **extra information** about the grandfather (*the strongest man I have ever known*), which shows how much the narrator admires him.

items.q: Why does the writer use a colon in line 2? (1 mark)
items.a: To introduce a **list** of the things they took fishing (*two rods, a bucket and a bag of bread*).

items.q: Why does the writer use a semicolon in line 3? (1 mark)
items.a: To **join two independent clauses that are closely related**: the line pulling and the rod bending happen together, so the reader sees how strong the fish is.

items.q: Why does the writer use a dash at the end of line 4? (1 mark)
items.a: To show an **interruption**: Grandad is cut off in the middle of speaking, which suggests something sudden has happened and creates tension.

items.q: Why does the writer use an ellipsis in line 5? (1 mark)
items.a: To create a **pause and suspense**: the reader has to wait before finding out what rises to the surface.

items.q: Find a comma used to separate the name of the person spoken to.
items.a: Line 4: *“Hold on, Sami!”*

items.q: Why does the writer use an exclamation mark in line 4?
items.a: To show that Grandad is shouting urgently, which shows his excitement or worry and makes the moment dramatic.

blocks.text: 17. Practice A: why does the writer use it?

items.q: *The old house (empty for twenty years) stood at the end of the street.* Why are brackets used?
items.a: To add extra information about the house: it has been empty for twenty years, which makes it seem mysterious.

items.q: *Something was moving in the garden... something big.* Why is an ellipsis used?
items.a: To create a pause and suspense before revealing that the thing is big. It makes the reader nervous.

items.q: *Nobody expected the winner – a seven-year-old girl.* Why is the single dash used?
items.a: For emphasis: it makes the surprising winner stand out after a short pause.

items.q: *The market was full of noise, colour, spices, people, cats and carts.* Why does the writer use so many commas?
items.a: To separate the items in a long list, which shows how busy and crowded the market is and builds a detailed picture.

items.q: *The so-called “shortcut” took us three hours.* Why are inverted commas used around *shortcut*?
items.a: To show the word is not meant literally: it was not really a shortcut, so it is funny and shows the writer's annoyance.

items.q: *“W-w-where are you going?” whispered Lina.* Why are hyphens used in *W-w-where*?
items.a: To show Lina is stammering, because she is frightened or nervous.

items.q: *Remember one thing: never feed the monkeys.* Why is a colon used?
items.a: For emphasis: it makes the important rule after it stand out.

items.q: *We missed the bus; we had to walk home in the rain.* Why is a semicolon used?
items.a: To join two independent clauses that are closely related: missing the bus and walking home are connected.

blocks.text: 18. Practice B: punctuate correctly

items.q: Add the missing punctuation: *where are you going asked dad*
items.a: *“Where are you going?” asked Dad.*

items.q: Add apostrophes: *The boys bikes were left outside the childrens library and they didnt lock them.* (more than one boy)
items.a: *The boys' bikes were left outside the children's library and they didn't lock them.*

items.q: Choose *its* or *it's*: *___ a lovely day. The bird is building ___ nest.*
items.a: *It's a lovely day. The bird is building its nest.*

items.q: Add a colon: *I have three hobbies reading, swimming and drawing.*
items.a: *I have three hobbies: reading, swimming and drawing.*

items.q: Add a pair of commas for extra information: *Mr Salah our maths teacher won a prize.*
items.a: *Mr Salah, our maths teacher, won a prize.*

items.q: Correct the speech: *“We are late.” said Mona “hurry up”!*
items.a: *“We are late,” said Mona. “Hurry up!”*

items.q: Is this semicolon correct? *Although it was cold; we went swimming.*
items.a: No. *Although it was cold* is not a complete sentence. Correct: *Although it was cold, we went swimming.*

items.q: Add hyphens: *My twenty two year old cousin is a well known singer.*
items.a: *My twenty-two-year-old cousin is a well-known singer.*

blocks.title: كيف تحصل على الدرجة في سؤال Why does the writer use...?
items: اكتب اسم العلامة + اقتبس الكلمات + الاستخدام (مثل: to add extra information) + الأثر على القارئ في هذا النص.
استخدم الإجابات المحفوظة في الصناديق الموجودة في هذه الصفحة فقط، ولا تخترع استخدامًا جديدًا.
في الكتابة: استخدم علامات متنوعة بشكل صحيح (colon و semicolon و brackets و dashes) لكن بدون مبالغة.
